lead: Etretinate (brand names Tegison, Tigason) is a second-generation oral retinoid developed by Hoffmann-La Roche for severe psoriasis and related keratinisation disorders. By slowing the over-production of skin cells that causes thick, scaly plaques, it was used to clear the visible lesions of severe disease. The US FDA approved it in 1986, and Roche voluntarily withdrew it from the Canadian market in 1996 and the US market in 1998 because of its very long elimination half-life and teratogenic potential.[1][2] Wikipedia lists it as still marketed in Japan.[1]

Its successor is acitretin, the free acid and an active metabolite, which has a much shorter half-life.[1][2][3] Etretinate belongs to the same family as isotretinoin and tretinoin, which are better known in appearance contexts through acne and anti-aging care. Within that family it was prescribed for skin disease rather than for cosmetic goals, and it appears in forum discussions mostly as a historical drug and in lists of drugs that affect pregnancy or blood donation eligibility.[7][8]

Published trials from the 1980s and early 1990s examined it in psoriasis, pustular psoriasis of the palms and soles, psoriatic arthritis, oral lichen planus and epidermal nevus, and reviews described it as one of the synthetic retinoids that made oral treatment of severe skin disease feasible.[4][9][10][11][12][13]

chain: Binds retinoid receptors in skin cells
Thick scaly plaques and hyperkeratosis flatten and clear in severe skin disease
angle.text: Etretinate was prescribed to clear the visible plaques, scale and thickened skin of severe psoriasis, ichthyosis and related disorders. Its influence on appearance came through treating disease rather than through cosmetic use, and it was withdrawn in North America in the 1990s.

infobox: Not marketed in the US or Canada; listed as marketed in Japan[1]

paras: Etretinate was used for severe recalcitrant psoriasis, including pustular and erythrodermic types, and for ichthyosis, Darier disease and pityriasis rubra pilaris.[2][4] Reviews of retinoid therapy describe it alongside isotretinoin as one of the synthetic retinoids that made oral treatment of severe skin disease feasible.[4][5] A 1988 review of retinoids and acne traced the history of retinoid use in acne and listed systemic etretinate among the agents considered.[9] It was also explored for chemoprevention of skin cancer and in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with evidence limited to small studies.[2] Reviews of acquired palmoplantar keratoderma and of cutaneous amyloidosis list retinoids including etretinate among reported treatment options.[14][15]

Combination approaches were common. Grokipedia says it was combined with PUVA phototherapy in resistant psoriasis and with methotrexate, with the aim of improving clearance while limiting side effects.[2]

Grokipedia summarises clinical trials as showing improvement of 75 to 90 percent in lesion severity after four to six months of treatment in many patients with plaque psoriasis, and about a 90 percent reduction in pustule counts after 12 weeks in palmoplantar pustulosis.[2] It reports response rates up to 80 percent within three months in Darier disease and clearing or substantial improvement in over two-thirds of treated cases of pityriasis rubra pilaris in small series.[2] These figures come from an AI-generated summary and should be read as approximate.

Reviews from the period describe the drug as effective for pustular forms and for hyperkeratotic disorders, with a response that could take weeks to appear.[4][5] A 1987 Medical Letter piece and an editorial in Archives of Dermatology from the same year discussed its place in psoriasis therapy when it was introduced.[10][16]

Effects resemble hypervitaminosis A: dry lips and skin, bone or joint pain, muscle cramps and dry eyes, with long-term use associated with hyperostosis.[1][2] Grokipedia also lists cheilitis, skin fragility, palmoplantar peeling, raised triglycerides, elevated liver enzymes, pseudotumor cerebri, corneal opacities and rare hepatotoxicity, particularly with methotrexate.[2] A 1986 letter in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology reported photosensitivity in a patient taking etretinate.[17]

Teratogenicity was a central concern. Etretinate is lipophilic, is stored in fat, and can be detectable in plasma for up to three years after therapy, so birth defects have been a risk long after treatment ends.[1][2] A 1986 review of vitamin A congeners recorded the teratogenic pattern seen with the retinoid class, including central nervous system, heart, ear, jaw and cleft palate defects after isotretinoin exposure in early pregnancy.[6] Former users are barred from donating blood in several countries, and a donation-eligibility list quoted on a T Nation forum states that anyone who has taken Tegison is not eligible at any time.[1][8]

Etretinate is metabolised to acitretin and acts on retinoid receptors to normalise keratinocyte differentiation.[1][2] Grokipedia describes agonism at retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors, formation of RAR-RXR heterodimers and altered transcription of genes controlling cell growth.[2] Absorption is increased by fat-rich meals, plasma protein binding is above 99 percent, and the elimination half-life of roughly 120 days and low therapeutic index made dosing difficult.[1][2]

A French review of acitretin states that acitretin has a terminal half-life of about 55 to 60 hours but that alcohol intake induces conversion to etretinate, with a terminal half-life of 84 to 168 days, which is why contraception is advised during treatment and for two years afterwards.[3] Acitretin can thus be partly converted back into etretinate in the body, which is the reason given for long pregnancy-avoidance periods after acitretin.[1][2][3]

Roche developed etretinate and the FDA approved it as Tegison in 1986, following the clinical introduction of isotretinoin for severe acne.[1][2][6] Withdrawal followed in Canada (1996) and the United States (1998), and acitretin was approved in the US in 1996 as a replacement.[1][2] The 1997 Drugs review looked back on 15 years of retinoid use, describing three generations of synthetic retinoids for psoriasis, keratinisation disorders, acne and cancer chemoprevention.[4]

Published clinical literature on etretinate is mostly from the 1980s and 1990s and is summarised in pharmacology and therapeutic reviews of retinoids.[4][5] Those reviews address psoriasis, ichthyoses and other hyperkeratotic disorders.

Individual trials include a double-blind controlled trial of etretinate (Tigason) against ibuprofen in psoriatic arthritis (1985), a placebo-controlled comparative trial of PUVA, etretinate and PUVA-etretinate combination in palmoplantar pustulosis (1987), a clinical trial of Tigason in symptomatic oral lichen planus (1992), and a controlled trial in inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus (1991).[11][12][13][18] The 1985 trial was double-blind and controlled, and the 1987 trial compared three regimens against placebo.[11][12] The abstracts available here do not give group sizes or outcome figures, so those results are not summarised. No studies of etretinate for cosmetic purposes were found.

timeline.event: Striking human teratogenicity findings emerge after isotretinoin marketing, shaping retinoid safety rules.[6]
Withdrawn in Canada; acitretin approved in the US.[1][2]

name: Etretinate

card.summary: A withdrawn oral retinoid for severe psoriasis, replaced by acitretin because it lingered in the body for years.
card.note: Withdrawn in the US and Canada; teratogenic risk persists for years after use.

quick.overview:
Etretinate was an oral vitamin A-derived drug for severe psoriasis, approved in the US in 1986 and withdrawn in the late 1990s.

It treated skin disease and was not a cosmetic; it has been replaced by acitretin.
quick.mechanism: It converts to acitretin and binds retinoid receptors to normalise skin-cell maturation. It is stored in body fat and has a half-life of about 120 days.
quick.risks: Because it persists for years, birth-defect risk lasts long after treatment. Other effects include dry skin and lips and bone or joint pain. It is no longer sold in the US or Canada.
